1F OurBigBook.com
An eigenvalue of a matrix A is a scalar λ for which Av=λv for some nonzero eigenvector v. Its corresponding eigenspace is
Eλ​=ker(A−λI).
(1)
Write v=(a,b,c,d)T. The displayed matrix is the outer product A=vvT, so
Ax=v(vTx)=v(v⋅x).
(2)
Its column space is contained in span{v} and is nonzero because Av=∥v∥2v=0. Hence A is a rank-one matrix.
The vector v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue ∥v∥2=a2+b2+c2+d2, and every vector in the orthogonal complement v⊥ has eigenvalue 0. Thus
E∥v∥2​=span{v},E0​=v⊥.
(3)
Since R4=span{v}⊕v⊥ is a direct sum of these eigenspaces, A has an eigenbasis and is therefore a diagonalizable.

∣f(x)−f(x0​)∣≤∣f(x)−fN​(x)∣+∣fN​(x)−fN​(x0​)∣+∣fN​(x0​)−f(x0​)∣<ε.

The Cauchy integral formula says that if f is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of the closed disc D(z0​;R)​, then for z∈D(z0​;R),
f(z)=2πi1​∫∣ζ−z0​∣=R​ζ−zf(ζ)​dζ.
(13)
In particular, at the centre,
f(z0​)=2π1​∫02π​f(z0​+reiθ)dθ
(14)
for every 0<r<R.
If f(z0​)=0, the assumed bound gives ∣f(z)∣≤0, so f=0. Otherwise define g=f/f(z0​). Then g(z0​)=1 and ∣g∣≤1. Applying the centre formula and taking real parts gives
1=2π1​∫02π​Reg(z0​+reiθ)dθ,Reg≤∣g∣≤1.
(15)
The continuous nonnegative function 1−Reg has integral zero, so it vanishes around the circle. Equality Reg=1 together with ∣g∣≤1 forces g=1. This holds for every r<R, hence f(z)=f(z0​) throughout the disc. This is the equality case underlying the maximum modulus principle.

On the other hand, writing each visit as an indicator random variable and applying the monotone convergence theorem to the partial sums gives
1+Ev​R=Ev​[∑n=0∞​1{Xn​=v}​]=∑n=0∞​Pv​(Xn​=v)=∑n=0∞​pvv​(n).

Let (xn​) be a Cauchy sequence in a compact metric space X. By sequential compactness of a compact metric space, it has a convergent subsequence xnj​​→x∈X. Given ε>0, choose N such that d(xm​,xn​)<ε/2 whenever m,n≥N, and then choose j such that nj​≥N and d(xnj​​,x)<ε/2. For every n≥N, the triangle inequality gives
d(xn​,x)≤d(xn​,xnj​​)+d(xnj​​,x)<ε.
(52)
Thus the whole sequence converges to x. Every Cauchy sequence converges in X, so X is a complete metric space.

ii OurBigBook.com
Let (xn​) be any sequence in a complete, totally bounded metric space X. Cover X by finitely many balls of radius 2−1; one contains infinitely many terms. From those terms choose an infinite subsequence lying in one ball of radius 2−2, and continue. The diagonal argument produces a subsequence (xnj​​) whose tail from its jth term onward lies in a ball of radius 2−j. Hence
d(xnk​​,xnℓ​​)<21−j
(55)
whenever k,ℓ≥j, so the subsequence is Cauchy. Completeness makes it converge in X.
Every sequence in X therefore has a convergent subsequence, so X is sequentially compact. Sequential compactness is equivalent to compactness for metric spaces, and thus X is compact. This proves that a complete totally bounded metric space is compact.

fn​(t)=⎩⎨⎧​0,2n​(t−21​+n1​),1,​0≤t≤21​−n1​,21​−n1​<t<21​+n1​,21​+n1​≤t≤1.​

These functions converge in the L1 norm to the step function h=1(1/2,1]​, because fn​−h is supported on an interval of length 2/n and bounded in absolute value by one. They are consequently Cauchy for the metric d, since for sufficiently close pairs the outer minimum with 1 does nothing.
If (fn​) converged in this metric to some f∈C[0,1], it would also converge to f in L1. Uniqueness of an L1 limit would give f=h almost everywhere. Continuity would then force f=0 on [0,1/2) and f=1 on (1/2,1], which is impossible at 1/2. Thus this Cauchy sequence has no limit in C[0,1], while every compact metric space is complete.

If ∼ is an equivalence relation on X and q:X→X/∼ is the natural projection, the quotient topology declares V⊆X/∼ open exactly when q−1(V) is open in X. For topological spaces X and Y, the product topology on X×Y has as a basis all sets U×V with U open in X and V open in Y.

Solution

b OurBigBook.com
A closed set C⊆X is compact because it is closed in the compact space X. Its image f(C) is compact by the fact that a continuous image of a compact space is compact, and every compact subset of the Hausdorff space Y is closed. Thus the continuous bijection f is a closed map. Its inverse f−1:Y→X is consequently continuous, so f is a homeomorphism. This is the compact-to-Hausdorff continuous bijection theorem.

Define a continuous map F:S→T by the standard embedded torus of revolution parametrization
F(s,t)=((2+cos2πt)cos2πs,(2+cos2πt)sin2πs,sin2πt).
(58)
Its image lies in T because
x2+y2​=2+cos2πt,(x2+y2​−2)2+z2=1.
(59)
The periodicity of the trigonometric functions makes F(s,0)=F(s,1) and F(0,t)=F(1,t), so F is constant on every ∼-equivalence class. The universal property of the quotient topology therefore gives a unique continuous map
F:S/∼⟶T,F([s,t])=F(s,t).
(60)
Every point of T has cylindrical radius between 1 and 3, so its polar angle determines s modulo one, while the pair (x2+y2​−2,z) on the unit circle determines t modulo one. Hence F is surjective, and two parameters have the same image exactly when they differ by the endpoint identifications defining ∼; thus it is injective.
The quotient S/∼ is compact as the continuous image of the given compact space S under the quotient map. The surface T is Hausdorff because it has the subspace topology inherited from R3. The compact-to-Hausdorff continuous bijection theorem now shows that F is a homeomorphism. Therefore
S/∼≅T​.
(61)

Given a hyperbolic line ℓ, choose a real Möbius transformation sending its two ideal endpoints to 0 and ∞. After multiplying its representing matrix by a scalar and, if necessary, changing its sign, it represents an element of PSL2​(R) and sends ℓ to the positive imaginary axis ℓ+​.
The chosen point P∈ℓ then maps to iy for some y>0. The dilation z↦z/y, represented by

The constant f=2Ωsinφ is the positive Coriolis parameter at northern latitude φ, g is the gravitational acceleration, and h is the undisturbed mean depth of the layer.
The linearized shallow water equations assume a homogeneous, incompressible, inviscid layer over a flat bed; a horizontal scale much larger than the depth, so the shallow-water approximation and hydrostatic approximation apply; depth-independent horizontal velocity; a free-surface displacement ∣η∣≪h and sufficiently small velocity to neglect nonlinear products; and an f-plane on which f is constant. The equations also omit viscosity, forcing, and bottom topography.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
The max-flow min-cut theorem states that in a finite flow network, the maximum value of a feasible source-to-sink flow equals the minimum capacity of a source-to-sink cut.
First consider any feasible flow f and any cut (A,V∖A) with S∈A and T∈/A. Summing flow conservation over the vertices in A cancels all contributions from edges internal to A and gives
∣f∣=∑u∈A,v∈/A​f(u,v)−∑u∈/A,v∈A​f(u,v)≤∑u∈A,v∈/A​c(u,v)=c(A,V∖A).
(139)
Thus every flow value is at most every cut capacity.
A maximum flow exists because the feasible flows form a nonempty compact subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and the flow value is continuous. Let f be maximum and form its residual network. If there were an augmenting path from S to T, increasing f by the path's positive bottleneck capacity would contradict maximality. Let A be the set of vertices reachable from S in the residual network. Then T∈/A. Every original edge from A to its complement is saturated, while every original edge entering A carries zero flow; otherwise the corresponding forward or reverse residual edge would make its other endpoint reachable. Consequently
∣f∣=∑u∈A,v∈/A​c(u,v)=c(A,V∖A).
(140)
The general upper bound is attained by this flow and cut, proving the theorem.

Solution

Words: 138
c OurBigBook.com
Assume the capacities are integers and begin with the zero flow. Inductively, if every edge flow is an integer, then every forward residual capacity c(u,v)−f(u,v) and reverse residual capacity f(u,v) is an integer. The bottleneck on an augmenting path is therefore a positive integer. Augmenting by it changes every affected edge flow by an integer, so all edge flows remain integral.
Each augmentation raises the flow value by at least one. On the other hand, every feasible flow satisfies
∣f∣≤∑v​c(S,v),
(149)
and the right side is a finite integer because the network is finite. There can therefore be only finitely many augmentations. When the algorithm stops, no augmenting path remains, and the source-reachable cut in the residual network has capacity equal to the current flow value. The max-flow min-cut theorem proves that the terminating flow is maximum. This proves both termination and the Integrality of the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm.
